lines.text: Pool the class's interview notes and a shared picture appears. The way food
is prepared — what we can call culinary practice — has changed sharply
within living memory.
Fifty years ago most Indian households cooked over a chulha burning wood,
dung cakes or coal (Fig. 3.1 a). Someone had to gather the fuel, light the fire,
and tend it. Today most households cook on a gas stove that lights in one
second and goes out in one second (Fig. 3.1b). Spices and grain were once
ground by hand on a sil-batta, a heavy stone slab worked with a stone roller
(Fig. 3.1 c). Now a mixer-grinder does the same work in a minute (Fig. 3.1d).
Why did all this change?
Partly because the technology arrived. Gas connections, electricity and
affordable appliances reached ordinary households, and once a tool that
saves an hour a day is available, people use it.
Partly because transport improved. Roads, railways and cold storage
mean that a fruit grown in Himachal can be sold in Chennai. Foods that
were once purely local became available everywhere, and cuisines began
to borrow from each other.
And partly because communication changed. Recipes now travel by
television, phone and internet. A dish that belonged to one region for
three hundred years can spread across the country in a season.
Change of this kind brings real gains. Cooking takes less time — which matters
most to the women who have historically done most of it. Fuel-efficient stoves
mean less smoke indoors, and less smoke means healthier lungs.
It also brings losses. Some traditional grains and dishes are disappearing, and
with them the knowledge of how to cook them. Some of those grains, as we
will see later in this chapter, were more nourishing than what replaced them.
WHY-IT-MATTERS
Smoke in the kitchen A wood or dung chulha burning indoors fills a
kitchen with fine smoke. Breathing that smoke for years damages the
lungs and the heart, and the person standing closest to the stove
breathes the most of it. This is one reason governments have worked
to bring clean cooking fuel to rural households: a better stove is a
health measure, not just a convenience.
